The first examination began before sunrise, when the shutters were closed and the lamp threw a narrow circle across the bench. I cleaned every contact, tightened the screws, and watched the brass dial tremble without settling upon a mark. The brass dial trembled after the current ceased. Nothing else moved. I entered the time, temperature, and pressure before disturbing the apparatus again.

During the second examination the assistant changed the cell, replaced the wire, and carried the instrument to the stone table by the eastern wall. His precautions occupied several minutes because each connection had to be inspected under a lens. When he restored the circuit, the pointer crossed half the scale and returned slowly. We compared our watches, repeated the current, and obtained a different movement that neither of us could explain.

At noon three observers joined us, bringing their own gauges and a sealed standard from the lower laboratory. The room had warmed, the window had been opened, and carts in the yard made the finer vibrations difficult to distinguish. Even so, the brass dial trembled in the same narrow arc. One observer called it friction. Another suspected the table. The third asked us to leave the mechanism untouched until evening.

We waited while the light shifted from the eastern windows to the high panes above the door. I used the interval to copy the earlier entries, including two doubtful readings and one interruption that the assistant had omitted. After the carts departed, we tested the table, floor, wall, and mounting separately. Each remained steady beneath a control instrument, yet our original apparatus continued its small irregular motion.

The final examination was made after dark with a fresh cell, a second lamp, and every loose article removed from the room. I stood at the bench while the others watched from several paces away. For a moment the pointer held at zero. Then the brass dial trembled once more, stopped, and trembled again. We sealed the instrument without assigning a cause, because repetition alone could not tell us whether we had found evidence, error, or a habit of observation.

My report therefore preserves the order of each trial rather than the confidence of any witness. The assistant believed the fault electrical, the first observer preferred a mechanical explanation, and the others declined to name one. I could add a smoother conclusion, but that would conceal the uncertainty recorded at the bench. The same unexplained movement appeared under altered conditions, and the same words returned whenever we tried to describe it.
